featureOneTitle: One coordinator. Work in every project.
featureOneDescription: A request can affect frontend, backend, and docs, leaving you to relay tasks and results. The coordinator uses product context to plan the work and dependencies, then follows up on reports from each project.
featureTwoTitle: Each project keeps its own development rules.
featureTwoDescription: Each project agent runs an independent native session in its project directory. Its own mechanisms load project instructions, Skills, hooks, and tools, reducing the risk of missing rules when work crosses projects.
featureThreeTitle: Different brands. One place to coordinate.
featureThreeDescription: Projects may rely on different agent brands whose instructions and tools are not interchangeable. Keep each existing setup, such as Codex for the frontend and Claude Code for the backend, while one coordinator connects their work. A coordinator running Claude Code can hand image generation to Codex, since Claude Code does not generate images, and can hand Codex the steps that drive a local application or a browser, where Codex is stronger, then continue from what Codex reports.
featureFourTitle: Join any project conversation. Steer the work.
featureFourDescription: Project details are easier to explain in the conversation doing the work. Talk directly to any project agent to add context, adjust requirements, or review code, while the coordinator follows overall progress.

privacySeoDescription: How {appName}, the agents you choose, and this website handle your information.
privacyIntro: This policy describes the current {appName} application and website. {appName} is an open source project operated by {operatorName}.
privacyLocalBody: The current version of {appName} runs on your device and stores the configuration and session data it manages locally. {appName} does not upload your code, conversations, or usage data to servers operated by its developer.
privacyAgentsTitle: Agents and tools from other providers
privacyAgentsBody: {appName} starts the coding agents you configure from other providers. These agents and their tools may send prompts, code, context, and other data to their service providers according to your configuration and actions. Their providers' privacy policies and terms apply to that processing. Repository operations may also connect to the Git remotes you configure, including when checking remote status.
privacySharingBody: To coordinate work, task descriptions, reports, and relevant context pass between participating sessions. When this information enters another agent's session, it may be processed by that agent's configured provider. Working with agents from different providers may therefore involve sharing task information with multiple providers.
privacyWebsiteBody: This is a static website hosted on GitHub Pages. We use a cookie to remember the language selected or detected for this browser for one year. We do not add analytics or advertising trackers. GitHub records visitors' IP addresses for security purposes; see GitHub's privacy statement.
privacyContactTitle: Information you choose to send us
privacyContactBody: If you contact us by email or through GitHub Issues, we receive the information you choose to provide and use it to respond to your request. Information posted in a public issue is visible to others. For privacy questions, contact {operatorName} at the email address below.
privacyFutureBody: Remote host support is planned and is not an available feature. This policy does not describe it.

faqOneAnswer: A request such as adding team invitations can require changes to the frontend, backend, and docs. Give it to a coordinating agent to organize work across those projects, track dependencies, and collect results, reducing the tasks and context you have to pass between sessions yourself.
faqTwoQuestion: Why not develop every project in one session, or have one agent use subagents?
faqTwoAnswer: Many agent workspace tools load the Skills and tools of several projects into a single session and develop them all there. The projects’ contexts get mixed, and the quality of the work becomes unpredictable. Working across directories or launching a subagent does not by itself guarantee that the target project’s full configuration is loaded either: when instructions or Skills depend on the parent conversation passing them along, rules can be missed; loading behavior varies by tool. {appName} starts an independent native session of the chosen agent in each project directory, so that agent loads local configuration through its own mechanisms while the coordinator organizes the work.
faqThreeQuestion: Can each project keep a different brand of agent?
faqThreeAnswer: Projects may already depend on different agent brands, and their instructions and tools are not interchangeable. Choose Claude Code, Codex, or Grok Build independently for the coordinator and each project; each keeps its own toolchain, while {appName} passes tasks, relevant context, and reports between sessions. A coordinator running Claude Code can ask Codex to generate an image, which Claude Code does not do, or to drive a local application or browser, where Codex is stronger, and then continue from what Codex reports.
faqFourQuestion: How do projects report back, and can I step in?
faqFourAnswer: A requirement or code detail may be easier to explain directly to the project agent doing the work. You can enter its conversation to add context, adjust requirements, or review code; sessions started by the coordinator still report results, open items, and decisions needed back to it.
faqFiveQuestion: Will the coordinator learn how my product fits together?
faqFiveAnswer: Ongoing conversations, project knowledge, and reports can help it understand your product and engineering structure, including which projects a request affects. That understanding depends on the context available to the session; keeping it up to date reduces repeated explanations.

faqSevenQuestion: What do I need, and what does it cost?
faqSevenAnswer: Install the agent CLIs you want to use. {appName} is free and open source under the MIT License. Those agents are yours, including one you point at a model you host yourself.
faqEightQuestion: Where do my code and conversations go?
faqEightAnswer: {appName} stores its application data locally and does not upload code or conversations to servers run by its developer. Your configured agents and tools may send data to their providers, collaboration may share task information with multiple providers, and Git operations may contact remote repositories; see the privacy policy for details.
faqNineQuestion: Can project agents run on a remote host?
faqNineAnswer: Not yet. Remote host support is planned and is not available.
